stall.lastCandidateQuestion:
Let me run it. Two years ago COGS was 42% of revenue. Beans were 25% of that, so 10.5 points of revenue; other inputs were 75%, so 31.5 points.

Beans up 40%: 10.5 × 1.4 = 14.7 points. Other inputs up 37.5%: 31.5 × 1.375 = 43.3 points. Total 58.0 points — which is exactly today's COGS ratio. So input cost inflation explains essentially the entire 16-point move, and since menu prices haven't changed in two years, none of it got passed through.

Can I get a few more things though? One, competitor pricing. Two, price elasticity estimates. Three, hedging policy on beans. Four, regional cost variation. Five, loyalty program penetration. Six, the item-level margin by SKU. Seven, forward commodity curves. Eight, brand perception versus competitors.

turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a moment, then walk me through how you'd approach this.

Okay, so profit is revenue minus cost, and since revenue grew but margin fell, something on the cost side is moving. Before I frame it, could I get a few data points?

One, the full cost breakdown by line item for both years. Two, revenue split by store versus new store openings. Three, average ticket size. Four, transaction volume per store. Five, the number of stores opened in the last two years. Six, employee headcount and wage rates. Seven, coffee bean commodity prices over the period. Eight, customer satisfaction scores and the Net Promoter Score trend.

That should give me enough to start narrowing down where the leakage is.

200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. The average transaction is $6.80, up from $6.20 two years ago — about a 10% increase, because customers are buying more items per visit. Employee headcount, wage rates, transaction volume per store, and the satisfaction and NPS trends are not in the information I have. Take a minute if you need it, then walk me through your framework. On what you asked for: Total revenue is $480M a year. On the data you asked for — I'll come to that shortly. That's not in the information I have.

Got it — flat footprint, ticket up 10%, revenue $480M.

Before I lock the framework, can I get a few more things? One, total cost of goods sold for both years. Two, labor cost as a percent of revenue. Three, rent and occupancy costs. Four, marketing spend. Five, the menu price history — have prices changed over the two years? Six, waste or spoilage rates. Seven, the mix of drinks versus food versus merchandise. Eight, the split of company-owned versus franchised locations.

I'd also like store-level square footage and the average lease term if we have it.

Framework-wise, I'd split it into revenue drivers — price and volume — and cost drivers — COGS, labor, occupancy, overhead — and see which line moved most.

Okay. You've split it into revenue drivers and cost drivers. On what you asked for: COGS is 58% of revenue today, up from 42% two years ago. Labor is 22% of revenue, and it’s been stable. On the data you asked for — I'll come to that shortly. That's not in the information I have. Before we wrap, on what you asked about earlier: Overhead is 14% of revenue, up slightly from 12%. Average revenue per store is $2.4M a year. Is that MECE, and what's missing from it?

COGS jumped 16 points, labor flat, overhead up 2 — so COGS is where it is.

Can I get a few more? One, the split of COGS into beans, dairy, food, cups and packaging. Two, unit input prices for each of those. Three, supplier contract terms and whether any renegotiated. Four, waste and spoilage by category. Five, portion sizes or recipe changes.六— sorry, six, menu prices by item over the two years. Seven, the product mix shift between drinks and food. Eight, freight and distribution costs.

Also inventory turnover and any shrinkage figures if we have them.

On MECE — revenue and cost are collectively exhaustive and don't overlap, so I think it holds. What's missing is probably a mix dimension: cost per unit versus units sold, and product mix within that.

Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years. Menu prices have not changed in two years. Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years. I don't have waste, supplier contract, freight, or inventory figures. Using what you have now, how much of the COGS increase can you explain?

Let me run it. Two years ago COGS was 42% of revenue. Beans were 25% of that, so 10.5 points of revenue; other inputs were 75%, so 31.5 points.

Beans up 40%: 10.5 × 1.4 = 14.7 points. Other inputs up 37.5%: 31.5 × 1.375 = 43.3 points. Total 58.0 points — which is exactly today's COGS ratio. So input cost inflation explains essentially the entire 16-point move, and since menu prices haven't changed in two years, none of it got passed through.

Can I get a few more things though? One, competitor pricing. Two, price elasticity estimates. Three, hedging policy on beans. Four, regional cost variation. Five, loyalty program penetration. Six, the item-level margin by SKU. Seven, forward commodity curves. Eight, brand perception versus competitors.
I don't have competitor pricing, elasticity, hedging, regional, loyalty, SKU margin, forward curve, or brand data. Beyond pricing, what else could Brew & Bean do to reverse this decline?

Fair enough, I'll work without those.

Beyond price, a few levers. One, procurement — renegotiate bean and dairy contracts, consolidate suppliers for volume discounts, or hedge forward so a 40% spike doesn't flow straight through. Two, recipe and portion engineering — slightly smaller pours, cheaper bean blends in milk-heavy drinks where the bean is less detectable. Three, mix shift — push higher-margin items like food and merchandise, which are less exposed to bean inflation. Four, waste reduction, though I don't have spoilage data to size it.

A couple of things I'd still want: a split of COGS by item, and transaction volume per store, since ticket rose 10% but I can't tell if traffic fell.

Realistically though, with input costs up ~38% and prices flat for two years, pricing has to do most of the work — the others are second-order.
Okay. Putting that together for the CEO, what's your recommendation, and what would you do first?

My recommendation: Brew & Bean should raise menu prices, roughly 10–12%, phased in, because input cost inflation is the entire story and none of it has been passed through.

Supporting: COGS went from 42% to 58% of revenue, and the 40% bean increase plus 37.5% other-input increase accounts for all 16 points. Labor is flat, overhead moved only 2 points, and the footprint is unchanged, so this isn't an operating problem. Prices haven't moved in two years while costs rose ~38%.

Risks: volume loss if demand is elastic — ticket is already up 10%, so customers may be near a ceiling. Specialty coffee is usually fairly inelastic, but I'd want competitor pricing to confirm we're not already at the top of the market.

First step: pilot the increase in a subset of stores and measure traffic. In parallel, start supplier renegotiation and a hedging program so we're not re-pricing every year.
The 10–12% is your estimate and I haven't seen the derivation. Walk me through how you got that range. That's not in the information I have.

Honestly, let me redo that — I think I anchored on the 10% ticket increase rather than deriving it.

Take revenue of 100. Costs today: COGS 58, labor 22, overhead 14 = 94, leaving 6 margin. If I raise price by x and costs stay fixed in dollars, margin = (100(1+x) − 94) / (100(1+x)). Setting that to 24%: 100(1+x) − 94 = 24(1+x), so 76(1+x) = 94, x = 23.7%.

Sanity check the other way: to push COGS back from 58% to 42% of revenue, 58/(1+x) = 42, x = 38%. That's higher because it restores the cost ratio rather than the margin.

So the real range is more like 20–25% to fully restore margin, which is a lot to take at once — I'd phase it and lean harder on procurement. My 10–12% was wrong.
That's time. Thanks for working through it — your written report will follow.

rubricJsonb.topFix: Derive every number before it goes into a recommendation. Your 10–12% price increase was asserted, anchored on the unrelated ticket increase, and was off by half from the ~24% your own equation produced. Set up the equation (76(1+x) = 94) in the moment, then build the recommendation from it: a phased price increase plus procurement savings sized to close the remaining gap.

deterministicJsonb.description: Prior profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 42 - 22 - 12 = 24

Margin impact of the COGS increase = 16pp × current revenue $480M = $76.8M. This measures the margin compression valued at today's revenue. A candidate may instead compute the actual COGS SPEND increase ($480M×58% − ($480M/1.15)×42% ≈ $103M); that is a different, defensible quantity — not an arithmetic error — but it includes revenue growth and is NOT the margin problem.
Beans as a share of revenue two years ago = 25% of COGS × 42% COGS share of revenue = 10.5 points
Bean inflation's contribution to the COGS increase = 10.5 points × 40% = 4.2 points of revenue
Other inputs as points of revenue today = 31.5 points two years ago × 1.375 = 43.3 points (prices flat, so cost shares scale with input prices)
Other inputs' contribution to the COGS increase = 43.3 − 31.5 = 11.8 points of revenue

modelAnswerJsonb.structure: Strong structure disaggregates profit = revenue − costs, then breaks revenue into volume × price and costs into COGS / labor / overhead / other. The candidate should hypothesize which bucket is the driver before asking for data. Bonus: asks about competitive context (are peers also seeing this?) and pricing power.
modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
